article.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

article.title: [gizmodo.com] AI-driven flaw discovery strains patching as outages hit US services
article.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

AI tools are rapidly uncovering software vulnerabilities and helping automate cyberattacks as outages disrupt U.S. email, flight operations, banking services and an internal National Security Agency communications network. Cybersecurity experts have linked some disruptions to rushed fixes for newly found flaws, but Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the incidents were separate operational problems and officials had no indication of malicious activity or a coordinated attack. Hackers are also using AI to automate attacks. The FBI said hackers used the Artex AI framework in attacks worldwide, with some gaining privileged access in under three hours, while Palo Alto Networks linked another framework, Cairn, to 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. Researchers also used AI to find Java4Shell, a flaw in Java’s Base64 decoding library that could let an attacker execute commands on a vulnerable server. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency urged organizations to patch it. U.S. regulators sent inquiries to banks affected by outages, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency plans a deeper review of the incidents. Canonical, the company behind Ubuntu, is separately offering AI-generated fixes to Ubuntu Pro customers through an optional early-release channel before its engineers complete normal review and testing.

article.title: [lemonde.fr] France orders poultry indoors as bird flu alert reaches highest level
article.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

France raised its bird flu risk classification for the mainland from moderate to high, the highest of three alert levels, effective Nov. 20. The order requires poultry to be kept indoors or otherwise protected from wild birds, with some exceptions allowing smaller or adapted outdoor areas. Authorities also tightened rules on poultry gatherings and certain bird movements. The Agriculture Ministry cited three confirmed outbreaks in backyard flocks since late October, infections among wild birds in France and rising cases along migration routes in neighboring countries. Officials fear the virus could spread from wild birds to commercial farms. France raised the alert from negligible to moderate earlier in November. The latest order follows detections in 24 European countries since Aug. 1, according to the animal-health surveillance bulletin.

Vaccination policy: Since autumn 2023, French farms keeping more than 250 ducks have been required to vaccinate them; experts say the program helped avert major outbreaks over the past two years (lemonde.fr, agri-mutuel.com). Past outbreak scale: France recorded 156 outbreaks on farms and in backyard flocks in the 2025-26 season, compared with thousands during the 2021-22 peak (agri-mutuel.com, 20minutes.fr). Farm costs: Lionel Candelon, president of the Gers Chamber of Agriculture, said vaccination costs are rising and warned that some farmers may eventually be unable to afford vaccination (ladepeche.fr). article.title: [bmj.com] Study finds limited code sharing as medical AI oversight faces scrutiny
article.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute reviewed nearly 4,000 clinical prediction studies and found that only about one in eight reported sharing code. Many public repositories also lacked documentation or files needed to run and check the analyses. The findings are intended to inform a guideline on reusable research code. A physician writing in The BMJ urged Utah to publish independently assessed counts of missed escalation cases before allowing AI-generated acne prescriptions to be reviewed after issuance rather than before. In South Korea, Doctors for a Fair Society called for scrutiny of possible AI-assisted cheating in a medical-school entrance exam, while the group’s leader cautioned against treating an individual’s high score or educational background as proof of wrongdoing.

In South Korea, Doctors for a Fair Society called for scrutiny of possible AI-assisted cheating in a medical-school entrance exam, while the group’s leader cautioned against treating an individual’s high score or educational background as proof of wrongdoing (kormedi.com). Study sample: Researchers drew from PubMed Central’s open-access collection and included studies that developed, updated or validated prediction models and cited the TRIPOD or TRIPOD+AI reporting checklists (lavx.hu). Safety reporting: Utah’s agreement sets a target of zero material missed escalations and requires audits of encounters the AI did not flag, but does not specify a count or denominator for quarterly public reporting (bmj.com). Exam scrutiny: The Korean group asked the consortium that administers the MDEET medical-school entrance exam for an official response. The test was not among 528 national qualification exams slated for a government-wide investigation (kormedi.com).

article.title: [stpetersburg.usf.edu] Study finds drought could cut cactus habitat by 80% by 2100
article.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

An international research team analyzed nearly 1,000 cactus species and found that more than a quarter could lose at least 80% of their suitable habitat by 2100 if severe droughts intensify. The researchers added drought projections to climate models, which commonly use long-term temperature and rainfall averages, and combined them with biodiversity records, field observations and community-science data. The projected losses could qualify affected species as Critically Endangered under criteria set by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), more than doubling the number of cacti in that category. Researchers say drought may also reduce growth or flowering without immediately killing plants, compounding threats from habitat destruction and illegal collection. The findings are expected to inform updated IUCN Red List assessments; the team says further research is needed to determine which life stages and biological processes drought affects.

article.title: [japantimes.co.jp] Climate change intensified Indonesia’s worst wildfires in a decade, study finds
article.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A World Weather Attribution study published Friday found that a strong El Niño drove Indonesia’s severe rainfall shortfall this year, while human-caused climate change made temperatures during the August-to-October fire season about 1.6 degrees Celsius higher. Researchers said warming made hot, dry fire conditions about three times more likely, while El Niño cut seasonal rainfall by roughly half. It was another successful year of Performances in the Park despite attendance being down, according to the Central Cariboo Arts and Culture Society. At a Nov. 25 Central Cariboo Joint Committee meeting, executive director Melissa Normandin provided an overview of the free, family-friendly summer concert series that brought live music and cultural performances in Boitanio Park for Williams Lake residents and visitors from July 9 to Aug. 27. An average of 219 attendees were welcomed each evening, marking a small decrease from the 2025 season that had an average weekly attendance of 237. “Attendance was a bit down and I’m going to blame the weather for that,” Normandin said. Of the 16 different performers or acts participating in this year’s Performances in the Park seven were local. A total program budget of $36,155 supported through diversified funding sources including local government, community sponsorships and in-kind contributions. In June, Williams Lake First Nation was added as a core funding partner with the City of Williams Lake and Cariboo Regional District for a three year term that includes an annual payment of $22,000 to the society for eight summer events. Normandin said their budget dollars were pretty consistent with previous years, and if they had more they could probably review some different asks received from the community including shade and covered areas. Cleanliness and adequately supplied washroom facilities throughout the evening was another challenge, along with glass, and broken bottles and garbage. “We can tackle that, and hopefully work with the city on that,” Normandin said. Mayor Surinderpal Rathor said he attended every concert and encouraged organizers to keep up the good work. The highest attendance was on Aug. 6 featuring Sassafrass (Kimberly Kavanagh) along with Punjabi Gidha and Punjabi Bhangra performances

article.title: [news.mit.edu] Older adults show weaker brain-clearing fluid waves during sleep
article.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

MIT researchers found that older adults had significantly weaker waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which helps clear waste from the brain during sleep, than younger adults. The researchers used brain imaging and electroencephalography to study volunteers ages 18 to 39 and 60 to 84, linking the reduced flow partly to weaker deep-sleep brain waves and diminished vascular responses. Separately, a study described in a paper shared on Reddit found that LSD-related gene-expression patterns in rats and mice ran counter to some patterns associated with human brain aging. LSD also reduced certain amyloid-beta-related changes in mouse brain-cell cultures. These are preclinical findings, not evidence that LSD prevents dementia in people.

article.title: [medicalxpress.com] Study links very large and small waists to higher death risk
article.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A study of more than 17 million South Korean adults found that both unusually large and unusually small waist measurements were associated with a higher risk of death across weight and age groups. The lowest observed risk was associated with waist circumferences of 80–94 centimeters in men and 75–89 centimeters in women. The association between waist circumference and death risk was stronger at older ages, especially among women 75 and older. Researchers analyzed routine health-check measurements from 2009–10 and tracked survival for nearly 14 years, through June 30, 2024. The study was observational and cannot show that waist size causes death. Among people with normal weight or overweight whose waist circumference was high for their body mass index (BMI), reducing waist circumference without necessarily losing weight appeared to offer a greater survival benefit than losing weight while reducing waist circumference, the authors said.

Risk increments: Among participants whose waists were at or above the average for their sex, age and BMI, each additional 5 centimeters was associated with a 16% higher death risk in men and 14% in women (medicalxpress.com, elnacional.com.do). Weight-loss findings: Among normal-weight participants with a large waist, neither a 5-centimeter waist reduction nor 8%–10% weight loss was generally associated with a lower death risk (medicalxpress.com). Other risk factors: Gastroenterologist Olga Sukhareva said insulin resistance can occur in people with low body weight and cited factors including low muscle mass, inactivity, diet, genetics and polycystic ovary syndrome (rambler.ru).
